question: A 29-year-old G1P0 female at 32 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding. She has had minimal prenatal care to-date with only an initial visit with an obstetrician after a positive home pregnancy test. She describes minimal spotting that she noticed earlier today that has progressed to larger amounts of blood; she estimates 30 mL of blood loss. She denies any cramping, pain, or contractions, and she reports feeling continued movements of the baby. Ultrasound and fetal heart rate monitoring confirm the presence of a healthy fetus without any evidence of current or impending complications. The consulted obstetrician orders blood testing for Rh-status of both the mother as well as the father, who brought the patient to the hospital. Which of the following represents the best management strategy for this situation?

options.opa: If mother is Rh-negative and father is Rh-positive then administer RhoGAM
options.opb: If mother is Rh-negative and father is Rh-negative then administer RhoGAM
options.opc: If mother is Rh-positive and father is Rh-negative then administer RhoGAM
options.opd: If mother is Rh-negative and father is Rh-positive, RhoGAM administration is not needed
options.ope: After 28 weeks gestation, administration of RhoGAM will have no benefit

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Rh-negative mother -> potential risk of Rh incompatibility -> need to administer RhoGAM if father is Rh-positive -> 95% CHAIN: Rh-negative mother -> RhoGAM administration if father's Rh status is positive -> 90% CHAIN: Rh-negative mother -> RhoGAM administration if father's Rh status is unknown -> 95%
analysis: The patient is Rh-negative and has experienced vaginal bleeding during pregnancy. In this scenario, RhoGAM administration is indicated to prevent Rh sensitization in case of fetal-maternal hemorrhage. RhoGAM is given to Rh-negative mothers who are carrying Rh-positive fetuses or whose partner is Rh-positive to prevent the development of Rh antibodies that could harm future pregnancies.
